I propose revising the report template to make exclusions visible without changing which runs contribute to the reported mean. The summary would show the mean alongside the number of runs attempted and the number retained. A separate table, labeled “Record of exclusions,” would account for the difference by listing each excluded run’s identifier, completion status, reason for exclusion, and whether a usable reading exists. Raw readings would remain in the underlying record, available through the existing review process.

The current summary lists only the runs used to calculate the mean. This makes the mean easy to read, but it prevents readers from distinguishing a batch with no exclusions from one whose exclusions have simply disappeared from view. The proposed table would make those decisions inspectable. It would not require excluded readings to enter the mean or alter the existing exclusion rule.

Two examples illustrate why that distinction matters. A run stopped because the temperature controller failed did not meet the stated measurement conditions. A completed run with an unusual result has not, for that reason alone, failed those conditions. Our existing rule therefore excludes controller failures and retains unusual completed results unless a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies exclusion. The table would show how that rule was applied.

The table must also include excluded runs that produced no usable reading. Listing only excluded numeric values would conceal those failures and could make a difficult batch appear cleaner than it was. At the same time, stopped runs should not be treated as measured outcomes. Reporting attempted and retained counts beside the mean would preserve that distinction while allowing readers to account for every run.

Greater visibility carries a risk: readers may try to calculate a new mean from everything reported. Clearly labeling the table and recording every exclusion reason may reduce that risk, but cannot eliminate it. Including every raw reading would add detail unnecessary to inspecting the exclusion decisions and could make those decisions harder to follow. The proposed fields therefore provide an account of exclusions while leaving access to raw readings within the existing review process.

The proposal also adds reporting work, especially when one fault affects several runs. A shared explanation could cover such a group, provided each affected run still appears and is linked to that explanation. This would reduce repeated prose while keeping the batch’s history countable.

The tradeoff remains greater transparency at the cost of additional work and some risk of misinterpretation. Reviewers would still need to judge whether the documented reasons are convincing: a fuller table cannot guarantee honest recording or resolve an ambiguous rule. It can make the decisions, including failures that yielded no reading, available for inspection.

The table would account for the difference, listing each excluded run’s identifier, completion status, reason for exclusion, and whether a usable reading exists. The current summary lists only the runs used to calculate the mean. This makes the mean easy to read, but readers cannot tell whether a batch had no exclusions or whether excluded runs were simply left out of the summary. The proposed table would make those decisions available for inspection. It would not change the exclusion rule or require every excluded reading to enter the mean.

For example, a run stopped because the temperature controller failed did not meet the stated measurement conditions. A completed run with an unusual result is different: the result alone does not establish that the conditions failed. Our existing rule excludes controller failures and retains unusual completed results unless a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies exclusion. The table would show how that rule was applied.

The table also needs to include runs with no usable reading. Listing only excluded numeric values would hide those failures and could make a difficult batch look cleaner than it was. Counting stopped runs as measured outcomes would create a different distortion. Reporting the numbers attempted and retained beside the mean, with the table explaining the difference, would distinguish attempts from the results used in the calculation.

Showing excluded runs might invite readers to calculate a new mean from everything they see. Labeling the table clearly and giving a reason for every exclusion would help explain the decisions, though it would not eliminate that risk. Reasons should not be omitted merely because they repeat. Including every raw reading is unnecessary for this purpose and could make the decisions harder to follow.

Reviewers would still need to judge whether the documented reasons are convincing. A fuller table cannot guarantee honest recording or repair an ambiguous rule. It would also take time to prepare, especially when one fault affects several runs. We could permit a shared explanation for such a group, while requiring each affected run to appear. That would reduce repeated prose and preserve an accurate count, but the tradeoff between fuller reporting and the work it requires would remain.

The committee should choose the handling replica for the navigation exhibit this season because it better fits the exhibit’s current question: how does a reading change when an instrument is tilted? Visitors cannot tilt the original. The replica would let them investigate that question directly, although whether the proposed activity helps them understand it remains to be tested.

The original’s availability on loan is a real opportunity, and one that may not recur. It offers something the replica cannot: a material connection to the instrument’s working history. A maker’s correction remains visible on its scale, providing a basis for an account of repair and adaptation. A photograph would not give every visitor the same experience as standing beside the object. These strengths support considering the original, but they do not establish that it best serves the exhibit we have designed. Our current text concerns reading and error. Making repair central would require a change in direction and a different use of the season’s remaining preparation time.

Cost supports the choice of the replica without deciding it. The loan would cost 18,000 units from the exhibit budget, including transport, insurance, and a sealed case. The replica would cost 7,000 units, including replacement parts for the season. Both fit the allocated budget, and neither quote is a complete estimate of staff time. The reason to prefer the replica is therefore what visitors would be permitted to do, not that the loan is unaffordable. Its lower quoted cost would also leave more resources available for testing the activity.

That testing is necessary. The replica’s moving parts could distract visitors from the question, or visitors could turn them without noticing the scale. A visitor trial has not yet happened, so we should not claim that handling has already improved understanding. The recommendation rests on the replica’s fit with the intended activity, not on a demonstrated teaching benefit.

Choosing the replica now would preserve the exhibit’s focus while leaving resources to test how well the activity works. We should retain a clearly labeled photograph of the original and explain why the replica can be handled. If the committee instead wants the original’s history to become the central question, it should explicitly authorize that change in the exhibit’s direction.

Let \(N\ge 2\), and let \(y_1,\ldots,y_N\) be fixed real responses. Define
\[
\mu=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N y_i,
\qquad
\sigma^2=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\mu)^2.
\]
Choose an unordered pair \(P\) uniformly from the \(\binom N2\) pairs, then choose \(J\) uniformly from the two indices in \(P\). Set
\[
Y=y_J,
\qquad
Z=\frac12\sum_{i\in P}y_i.
\]
All expectations and variances below refer to this sampling procedure; the population responses are fixed. We show that
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\]

Each index \(i\) belongs to \(N-1\) pairs. Thus
\[
\Pr(J=i)=\frac{N-1}{\binom N2}\cdot\frac12=\frac1N.
\]
Consequently, \(Y\) is a uniformly sampled population response, so
\[
\mathbb E[Y]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sigma^2.
\]

Conditional on \(P=\{i,j\}\), the variable \(Y\) takes the values \(y_i\) and \(y_j\) with equal probabilities, while \(Z=(y_i+y_j)/2\) is fixed. Hence
\[
\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z,
\qquad
\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]=0.
\]
Averaging the first identity over the possible pairs gives
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[Y\mid P]\right]
=\mathbb E[Y]=\mu.
\]

To obtain the variance, write
\[
Y-\mu=(Y-Z)+(Z-\mu).
\]
The cross term has expectation zero. Indeed, conditioning on \(P\) makes \(Z-\mu\) a fixed multiplier, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
&=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)\mid P]\right]\\
&=\mathbb E\!\left[(Z-\mu)\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]\right]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Squaring the decomposition and taking expectations therefore yields
\[
\sigma^2
=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+\operatorname{Var}(Z).
\]
This step uses the zero conditional mean of \(Y-Z\), not independence of \(Y\) and \(Z\).

For a given pair \(P=\{i,j\}\), the two possible values of \(Y-Z\) are \((y_i-y_j)/2\) and its negative. Therefore,
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2\mid P=\{i,j\}]
=\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
\]
Averaging over the uniformly chosen pairs gives
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
=\frac{1}{4\binom N2}\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2.
\]
Expanding the squared differences establishes the finite-population identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
&=N\sum_i y_i^2-\left(\sum_i y_i\right)^2\\
&=N\sum_i(y_i-\mu)^2
=N^2\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
It follows that
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]=\frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)},
\]
and hence
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(Z)
=\sigma^2-\frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)}
=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.}
\]

When \(N=2\), the pair contains the entire population and \(Z=\mu\) is constant. If all responses coincide, both variances vanish for every \(N\). The argument covers these cases without dividing by \(\sigma^2\).

Let \(N\geq 2\), and let \(y_1,\ldots,y_N\) be fixed real responses. Write
\[
\mu=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N y_i,
\qquad
\sigma^2=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\mu)^2.
\]
Choose an unordered pair \(P\) uniformly from the \(\binom{N}{2}\) pairs, then choose \(J\) uniformly from the two indices in \(P\). Set
\[
Y=y_J,
\qquad
Z=\frac12\sum_{i\in P}y_i.
\]
We will show that
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\]
All expectations and variances concern repeated sampling from the fixed population.

Each index \(i\) belongs to \(N-1\) pairs. Hence
\[
\Pr(J=i)
=\sum_{\substack{p:\,i\in p\\ |p|=2}}
\Pr(P=p)\Pr(J=i\mid P=p)
=\frac{N-1}{2\binom{N}{2}}
=\frac1N.
\]
Thus \(J\) is uniform on the population, so
\[
\mathbb E[Y]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sigma^2.
\]

Conditional on \(P=\{i,j\}\), the variable \(Y\) takes the values \(y_i\) and \(y_j\) with equal probabilities. Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[Y\mid P=\{i,j\}]=\frac{y_i+y_j}{2},
\]
which means that \(\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z\). Taking expectations gives
\[
\mathbb E[Z]
=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[Y\mid P]\right]
=\mathbb E[Y]
=\mu.
\]

To relate the two variances, write
\[
Y-\mu=(Y-Z)+(Z-\mu).
\]
Because \(Z\) is determined by \(P\),
\[
\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]
=\mathbb E[Y\mid P]-Z
=0.
\]
We can therefore condition on \(P\) and take the factor \(Z-\mu\) outside the conditional expectation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
&=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)\mid P]\right]\\
&=\mathbb E\!\left[(Z-\mu)\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]\right]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is an orthogonality relation and does not require \(Y\) and \(Z\) to be independent. Expanding the square now yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2
&=\mathbb E[(Y-\mu)^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
  +2\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
  +\mathbb E[(Z-\mu)^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+\operatorname{Var}(Z).
\end{aligned}
\]

It remains to compute the first term. Conditional on \(P=\{i,j\}\), the difference \(Y-Z\) equals either \((y_i-y_j)/2\) or its negative. Thus
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2\mid P=\{i,j\}]
=\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
\]
The sum of these squared differences satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
&=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N(y_i-y_j)^2\\
&=N\sum_{i=1}^N y_i^2-\left(\sum_{i=1}^N y_i\right)^2\\
&=N\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\mu)^2\\
&=N^2\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Averaging over the uniformly chosen pair gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
&=\frac{1}{4\binom{N}{2}}\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2\\
&=\frac{N^2\sigma^2}{4\binom{N}{2}}
=\frac{N}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Z)
=\sigma^2-\frac{N}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2
=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\]

When \(N=2\), the pair is the full population and \(Z=\mu\) is constant. If all responses coincide, both variances vanish for every \(N\). The proof requires no division by \(\sigma^2\).
